text.p: Deutsche Lufthansa AG said on Wednesday it will shed at least 10 percent of management staff in a revamp to prepare for increased competition after full liberalisation of the European aviation market this year.
Shares in the German national carrier surged almost six percent on the news, trading up 1.30 marks at 23.45 marks in early afternoon trade.
Lufthansa, due to be fully privatised at the end of the year, said it will group all its passenger services in a separate division which will act as a profit centre with its own management board.

The move marks the completion of a restructuring begun in 1994 and takes effect on April 1, coinciding with the implementation of an open skies agreement which will allow airlines to compete for all routes in Europe.
The airline said in a statement it would be creating a wide-ranging passenger division under which sales, marketing, network management, flight and staff operations would be brought together.

The division's six-member management will report to the group board which will be free to concentrate on steering the airline as a whole, ensuring "greater market proximity, flexibility and homegeneity of leadership," the statement said.

The announcement scotched media speculation that the airline was planning to hive off its scheduled passenger services into a separate subsidiary, to be called Passage AG, and to set up a holding company.
A source close to the company said aviation authorities would not have approved such a spin-off because Lufthansa needed to retain its legal status as a scheduled airline.

The addition of a management layer contrasts with a reorganisation at industrial giant Daimler-Benz AG which said last month it was scrapping the management board of its car subsidiary Mercedes-Benz AG in an internal merger.
Meanwhile Lufthansa's chief executive Juergen Weber told Reuters the cost of the changes had already been budgeted for as part of a wider cost-saving programme that began in 1994.
He added he believed staff would accept the measures and said it was "much too early" to assess what cost savings they would result in.

Analysts gave a cautious welcome to the changes but added the savings were likely to be relatively small and that Lufthansa's share could come under pressure when it publishes what will almost certainly be weaker earnings for 1996.
In addition, the threat of a strike by Lufthansa air and ground staff over a wage dispute continues to loom, with white-collar DAG conducting a strike ballot.
And when the skies open in April, Lufthansa will be confronted with competitors like British Airways and KLM which have worked just as hard to cut costs, analysts said.

"It makes sense if responsibility for costs and earnings is placed with a new layer of management and it makes sense to combine activities which belong together under one management," said Uwe Weinreich, aviation analyst at BHF-BANK.
But Heinz Weyershaeuser at DG Bank said: "It doesn't necessarily mean they will become more efficient in their operating business. I would see Lufthansa's change as neutral."
